text: Almost every statistical analysis starts from the same uncomfortable fact: you rarely see everything. You want to know about all your customers, but you only have some of them. This lesson introduces populations and samples, shows with simulation how much a sample can wander from the truth, and shows how a badly collected sample can be wrong in a way that no amount of extra data fixes.

The population is the complete group you care about. A sample is the subset you actually observe. A number describing the population, like its true average spend, is a parameter. A number computed from the sample is a statistic, used to estimate the parameter. Parameters are fixed but usually unknown; statistics change from sample to sample.

Simulating 100,000 customers with a region, orders per year, and annual spend — something you'd never actually see in real work, but it lets us check our answers here. The true population mean spend comes out to 170.22. That's the parameter.

A simple random sample gives every member an equal chance of selection. Taking five separate samples of 200 customers gives five different estimates, ranging from 159.2 to 180.3. None of them is wrong — they just reflect random luck. This is sampling variability, and crucially, random error has no systematic lean up or down; it averages out.

Sampling bias is different — a systematic tilt caused by how you collect the data. Suppose you email a survey and only customers with 6 or more orders a year bother to respond, 37 percent of customers here. Even with 2,000 respondents, the estimate comes out to 241.55, far above the true 170.22. That's selection bias, and collecting 20,000 respondents from the same group wouldn't repair it — it would only make you more precisely wrong.

A close cousin is voluntary response, where people opt in and the ones who do are unusual. If the chance of responding is proportional to spend, the estimate comes out to 250.05 — about 47 percent too high. Other classic biases include survivorship bias, only looking at customers who stayed, and undercoverage, where your list misses part of the population entirely.

Simple random sampling is the baseline. Stratified sampling splits the population into groups and samples within each, guaranteeing proportional representation — sampling 200 this way gives 100 North, 60 South, 40 West, matching the population's actual split, and lands much closer to the truth at 174.39. Cluster sampling picks whole groups and is cheaper but noisier; convenience sampling, using whoever is easy to reach, is common and risky.

Most analysts inherit data rather than design the sampling themselves. Always ask: who is missing from this data, and why? Who chose to be in it? A dataset of logged-in users says little about people who never log in. To recap: a statistic estimates a parameter, random error is unavoidable but averages out and shrinks with more data, and bias comes from how the data was collected — it does not shrink with more data. Fix bias with design, not volume.
